content: The California School for the Blind is a public educational institution located in Fremont, California, serving blind children from kindergarten through 12th grade. It is situated adjacent to the California School for the Deaf. History The education of blind children in the San Francisco area began in 1860 with the establishment of the Society for the Instruction and Maintenance of the Indigent Deaf and Dumb, and the Blind in California. This organization was founded by Mrs. Frances Clark, who served as the school’s first principal until 1865. Dr. Warring Wilkinson succeeded her and initiated efforts to transition the school to full state support. Under his leadership, the school, then known as the California State Asylum for the Deaf, Dumb, and Blind, relocated to Berkeley in 1867. In 1906, an amendment to the Political Code renamed the institution the California Institution for the Deaf and Blind, officially integrating it into the California State school system. Dr. Wilkinson retired in 1910. In 1914, the Legislature replaced the term Institution with School, renaming it the California School for the Deaf and Blind. In 1922, the school was divided into two separate programs: the California School for the Blind (CSB) and the California School for the Deaf. However, the formal separation was not completed until 1929, when a new classroom building was finished. In 1943, the California School for the Blind received authorization from the state legislature to admit deaf-blind students, becoming the third school in the United States to establish a program for this population. The first deaf-blind student graduated from the school in 1949. Enrollment at the school peaked in 1965 with 167 students. By 1973, the California Department of Education determined that the school needed to relocate to a more accessible site that could accommodate students with limited mobility and meet updated earthquake and fire safety standards. A new campus was constructed in Fremont, and the school moved there in 1980. Campus Berkeley (1867–1980) The original Berkeley campus featured a Victorian Gothic stone building constructed in 1867, which was destroyed by fire in January 1875. Temporary buildings were used for classes until new facilities were built, including an educational building, four dormitories, support facilities, and a private residence for the principal. In 1890, a Spanish Colonial Revival-style education building was completed, featuring an assembly hall and a 160-foot tower with a Seth Thomas clock. This building survived the 1906 San Francisco earthquake with only minor damage to chimneys, the slate roof, and some interior walls. Over the years, additional structures were added to the campus, including a gymnasium in 1915, a girls' dormitory in 1925, a boys' dormitory and another classroom building in 1929, an extension to the classroom building in 1931, the Helen Keller Building for deaf-blind education in 1949, and a new dining facility in 1957. Helen Keller herself attended the dedication of the building named in her honor. In the 1970s, plans were made to relocate the school to Fremont, and the move was completed in 1980. The Berkeley campus was designated a Berkeley Landmark in 1981 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. The former site was divided between the University of California and the city of Berkeley. In 1986, the university opened its portion as the Clark Kerr Campus residential complex, while the city opened its portion as Redwood Gardens, a housing facility for low-income elderly residents. Fremont (1980–present) The school’s current campus in Fremont was designed to meet modern accessibility standards and provide updated facilities for students with visual impairments. Curriculum The California School for the Blind follows a nationally recognized expanded core curriculum tailored to the needs of blind and visually impaired students. Extracurricular Activities Students at the California School for the Blind participate in a variety of extracurricular activities, including swimming, karate, goalball, tandem bicycling, music groups, dance groups, art, cooking, roller skating, and international pen pal exchanges via audio recordings. Many students are also members of the Alameda County Special Olympics team and the United States Association of Blind Athletes. Notable Alumni Dr. Newel Perry, a prominent alumnus of the California School for the Blind, was the founder of the California Council of the Blind. This organization was one of the original seven state groups that helped establish the National Federation of the Blind.
